strengths: Provides a unified theoretical framework covering a wide range of practical stochastic optimizers (SignSGD, Signum, Normalized-SGD, Spectral-SGD, Muon, and their variance-reduced variants) as instances of mini-batch steepest descent under different norms, extending prior full-batch-only implicit bias analyses (e.g., Fan et al. 2025) to the more practically relevant stochastic setting.

Delivers a coherent set of results characterizing how batch size and momentum trade off to determine whether the stochastic algorithm recovers the full-batch max-margin implicit bias, including explicit convergence rates for various learning-rate decay schedules.

The variance-reduction result (recovering the exact full-batch margin for any batch size, at the cost of slower rates) is a clean and intuitive theoretical contribution that ties together the batch-size and momentum findings.

Removes the polynomial dimension dependence present in the closest prior work (Fan et al. 2025) via a sharper entrywise-norm gradient-difference bound, which is a genuine, clearly explained technical improvement.

The batch-size-one analysis on a specially constructed orthogonal dataset is a nice counterexample showing per-sample steepest descent can converge to a qualitatively different (frequency-averaged, not margin-based) solution, which is a conceptually interesting and somewhat surprising finding that tempers the main narrative.
Extension to exponential loss and detailed, largely self-contained proofs in the appendix suggest technical thoroughness and reasonable reproducibility of the theoretical claims.

Synthetic experiments span all algorithm variants (with/without momentum, with/without VR) and three norm geometries (ℓ2, ℓ∞, spectral), and qualitatively corroborate the theoretical predictions (breakdown under small batch without momentum, restoration with large momentum or VR).
weaknesses: All theoretical results are restricted to linear multi-class classifiers on linearly separable data; despite motivating the work through LLM pretraining and Muon/Adam, there is no theoretical or empirical treatment of nonlinear/neural architectures, which substantially limits the practical significance of the claims.

Experiments are entirely synthetic and very small scale (n=200, d=5, 10 classes), with no validation on real datasets or realistic neural network training despite the paper's motivation being large-scale LLM optimization; this leaves a large gap between the paper's stated motivation and its empirical support.

The convergence bounds involve many compounding constants (R, n, m, batch-dependent exponents like m^{2+a}) and rely on reaching a possibly very large threshold time t2 before the stated rates apply; there is little discussion of how large these thresholds/constants are in practice or whether the bounds are informative at realistic scales.

The batch-size-one result, while conceptually interesting, is established only for a specially constructed orthogonal, scale-skewed dataset; it is unclear how much this generalizes to realistic data distributions, and the paper acknowledges this limits any unified theory for the small-batch regime.

The random-reshuffling assumption and momentum drift analysis rely on several technical assumptions (3.3, 3.4) whose practical scope (beyond polynomial learning-rate schedules) is not extensively discussed or justified beyond citing that they are 'commonly used.'

Given the substantial overlap in spirit with concurrent work (Baek et al. 2025 on per-sample Adam), the paper's novelty is somewhat incremental in framing, even though the technical execution (dimension-free rates, general norms, VR analysis) differs and improves upon it.

The paper's presentation is very dense, with the main text mostly summarizing results whose substance and nuance are deferred to a ~50-page appendix; some threshold-time and constant definitions (e.g., t0, t1, t2) are introduced somewhat implicitly and could be clarified for readability.

strengths: The paper provides a genuinely unifying theoretical framework covering a wide range of practically used optimizers (SignSGD, Normalized-SGD, Muon, Spectral-SGD) as instances of norm-induced steepest descent, and systematically studies how batch size, momentum, and variance reduction affect their implicit bias -- this is a natural and useful extension of the full-batch analysis of Fan et al. (2025).

The technical machinery (Appendix C-I) is extensive and internally consistent: explicit non-asymptotic margin convergence rates are derived for several regimes (no-momentum large-batch, momentum small-batch, variance-reduction, and per-sample batch-size-one), with matching rates recovering prior full-batch results as special cases.

The removal of the explicit dimension dependence d present in Fan et al. (2025)'s rate (replacing entrywise coordinate bounds with global ℓ1-norm gradient-difference bounds) is a legitimate, if incremental, technical improvement.

The batch-size-one counterexample (Theorem 4.9) is a nice qualitative result showing that per-sample steepest descent can converge to a fundamentally different (frequency-averaged) bias rather than a max-margin solution, illustrating a genuine limitation of naive SGD that is corroborated by small synthetic experiments.
The paper extends the analysis to the exponential loss and provides fairly complete proof appendices, suggesting reasonable technical rigor.
weaknesses: There is a large gap between the stated motivation (understanding practical large-scale LLM pretraining optimizers such as Adam, AdamW, and Muon) and the actual validation, which is restricted to a tiny synthetic multi-class linear classification problem (10 classes, 20 samples/class, feature dimension d=5). No experiments involve nonlinear models, real data, or even moderate-scale linear problems, so it is unclear whether the theoretical predictions have any bearing on the motivating applications.

The 'large-batch' condition required for convergence without momentum, b > 4Rn/(γ+4R), is very restrictive and in many realistic margin/data regimes effectively forces near full-batch training; the paper does not discuss how tight or vacuous this condition is for realistic data distributions (e.g., growing n with fixed margin), which undermines the claimed practical relevance of the 'batch-momentum trade-off' story.

The batch-size-one counterexample relies entirely on a specially constructed orthogonal, scale-skewed dataset with W0 = 0 initialization; the authors themselves acknowledge this is a narrow construction, and it is unclear how representative or generalizable this finding is beyond this toy setting, weakening the strength of the claimed 'fundamentally different implicit bias' conclusion.

The convergence-rate results are heavily parameterized by m = n/b, β1, a, and various problem constants (R, γ) in complex, hard-to-interpret combined forms (e.g., Corollary 4.5/4.7/G.5); the paper offers little practical guidance or intuition for readers on how to actually choose batch size or momentum in practice, despite this being advertised as a central contribution.

The core theoretical contribution is largely an incremental (albeit nontrivial) extension of Fan et al. (2025) from full-batch to mini-batch/momentum/variance-reduction settings using fairly standard proof techniques (Taylor expansion + proxy function G(W) + Random-Reshuffling zero-sum arguments); the conceptual novelty is modest relative to the very large volume of technical machinery required.

Experiments only report qualitative convergence curves (relative error, cosine similarity) without any quantitative comparison to the derived theoretical rates, so the tightness or practical predictive power of the many rate bounds (Corollaries 4.2, 4.5, 4.7, G.5) is never empirically verified.

The Random Reshuffling (sampling without replacement) requirement is a nontrivial restriction relative to standard with-replacement mini-batch SGD used in most practical deep learning pipelines, which is not adequately flagged as a limitation given how central this assumption is to the zero-sum-epoch proof technique (Lemma C.12).

strengths: The paper presents a unified and general theoretical framework for the implicit bias of mini-batch stochastic steepest descent under general entry-wise and Schatten-p norms, covering practically relevant optimizers (SignSGD/Signum, Normalized-SGD, Spectral-SGD/Muon) as special cases.

The results are comprehensive and tell a coherent story: they characterize precisely when stochastic training recovers the full-batch max-margin implicit bias (large batch, or with momentum, or with variance reduction), and when it fundamentally departs from it (small batch without momentum/VR), with explicit convergence-rate corollaries for common learning-rate schedules.

The momentum analysis achieves a genuinely improved, dimension-free convergence rate relative to prior work (Fan et al., 2025), which is a nontrivial technical contribution (obtained via tighter entrywise ℓ1-norm control of gradient differences rather than coordinate-wise bounds).

The batch-size-one analysis with the orthogonal scale-skewed dataset construction is a nice concrete example showing a qualitatively different implicit bias (sample-averaging bias vs. margin-driven bias), which is an interesting and illustrative negative result rather than only positive convergence claims.

The technical work is extensive and detailed, with many supporting lemmas (proxy function properties, stability of gradients/Hessians, mini-batch noise bounds, momentum accumulation bounds, explicit t0/c2 constants for the key assumption) that support reproducibility of the proofs.

Empirical results across ℓ2, ℓ∞, and spectral norms, with multiple batch/momentum/VR configurations, are broadly consistent with the theoretical predictions, and additional experiments validate the batch-size-one bias theorem directly.
weaknesses: The setting is restricted to linear multi-class classifiers on linearly separable data with cross-entropy/exponential loss; while this mirrors prior implicit-bias literature, it limits direct applicability to nonlinear/deep models, which the authors acknowledge only briefly as a limitation.

The batch-size-one result (Theorem 4.9) is established only for a specially constructed orthogonal scale-skewed dataset, so it is unclear how representative or generalizable this qualitative departure from full-batch bias is for more realistic data distributions.

The bounds contain several problem-dependent constants (e.g., c2 from Assumption 3.4, R, n, m) whose dependence on β1, m, a can become quite large (e.g., blow-up as β1→1 or for small a), and while Lemma C.15 provides explicit Big-O forms, the practical tightness/usefulness of these bounds for realistic hyperparameters is not clearly demonstrated.

The experiments are conducted only on small synthetic datasets (n=200, d=5, or n=500, d=10); there is no empirical validation on any real dataset or larger-scale/neural setting, which would strengthen confidence that the theoretical phenomena persist in more practical regimes.

The large-batch condition without momentum (b > 4Rn/(γ+4R)) may be quite conservative/pessimistic in practice, and the paper does not provide empirical evidence characterizing how tight this threshold is relative to actual convergence behavior observed in experiments.

Some of the rate comparisons (e.g., momentum slows convergence, VR slows convergence) are somewhat expected/intuitive trade-offs from a high level, and the paper could more clearly state which quantitative aspects are genuinely surprising versus confirmatory of known intuitions from convex optimization noise-reduction trade-offs.

strengths: Addresses a novel and timely gap: extending implicit bias theory of norm-induced steepest descent (SignSGD, Muon, Normalized-SGD) from full-batch to the mini-batch stochastic setting, relevant to modern LLM optimizers.
Unified framework covering a wide range of algorithms and stabilization mechanisms (momentum, SVRG-style variance reduction) under general entry-wise/Schatten-p norm geometries.
The negative result on lack of momentum (full-batch necessity) is substantiated by a concrete, rigorous counterexample at m=2 (Proposition 4.2), not just a loose sufficient condition.
Technical improvement of independent interest: removes dimension dependence present in prior work (Fan et al. 2025) via tighter global norm bounds on gradient differences.
Extensive theoretical apparatus with detailed, careful appendix proofs, including explicit non-asymptotic constants (e.g., Lemma C.15) supporting reproducibility of theoretical claims.
Reasonably thorough empirical validation across three norms and multiple batch/momentum settings on synthetic data, plus a supporting MNIST experiment with a two-layer nonlinear network.
weaknesses: Entire analysis restricted to linear classifiers on linearly separable data; the practical motivation (deep network training with Muon/SignSGD) is not theoretically covered, and the MNIST experiment (two-layer nonlinear network) is only an empirical, unsupported extension.

The batch-size-1 implicit bias result (Theorem 4.10) relies on a specially engineered orthogonal scale-skewed dataset, limiting generality; the broader claim that no unified small-batch implicit bias theory exists is only suggestively, not rigorously, supported.

Derived convergence rates are complex and involve conservative multiplicative factors (e.g., m/(1-β1), m^{2+a}/(1-β1)) without matching lower bounds, making it hard to assess tightness or practical relevance.

Significant technical machinery (proxy function G(W), core geometric lemmas) is directly inherited from Fan et al. 2025's full-batch framework, making the overall proof architecture incremental; novelty is concentrated in the stochastic noise/momentum/SVR bias bounding lemmas.

Some derived conditions for momentum to help are impractically restrictive (e.g., 1-β1 = O(n^{-3}) needed for b=Ω(1)), and the paper does not discuss whether commonly used momentum values would satisfy the theoretical guarantees for realistic dataset sizes.
Experiments confirm qualitative trends but do not quantitatively verify the tightness or specific scaling (in n, m, β1) of the derived theoretical rates.
Dense notation and heavy reliance on forward references to appendix-defined constants reduce readability of the main text.

strengths: The paper presents a unified theoretical framework covering a wide range of practically used optimizers (SignSGD/Signum, Normalized-SGD, Spectral-SGD/Muon) as instances of steepest descent under different norms, and systematically studies how batch size, momentum, and variance reduction interact to shape implicit bias -- a timely question given the practical adoption of Muon-like optimizers.

The technical contribution removing the dimension dependence present in Fan et al. (2025)'s rate (e.g., O(log t + n)/t^{1/2} vs. O(d log t + nd)/t^{1/2}) is a genuine and non-trivial improvement, achieved via a cleaner global ℓ1-norm gradient-difference argument.

The concrete counterexample (Proposition 4.2) showing that random-reshuffling SignSGD without momentum fails to classify correctly already at m=2 is a clean, convincing negative result that substantiates the claim that the large-batch condition is not just a proof artifact.

The proofs are extremely detailed and self-contained (75+ pages of appendix), with careful handling of stochastic/momentum/variance-reduction interactions, extension to exponential loss, and empirical validation on both synthetic data and a two-layer network on MNIST.
weaknesses: The headline no-momentum result (Theorem 4.1) is essentially degenerate: the 'large-batch condition' is shown to force m=1 (i.e., full-batch) under the stated assumptions, meaning the theorem does not actually establish a meaningful large-but-not-full-batch guarantee. The positive content of Section 4.1 is thus mostly negative/collapse results, which is a fairly weak center-piece for the paper's main technical section.

The whole analysis is restricted to linear multi-class classifiers on linearly separable data with random reshuffling under quite technical learning-rate assumptions (3.3, 3.4) whose practical satisfaction and tightness are not intuitive; this greatly limits the significance of the claims for realistic deep-learning training regimes despite framing the work around LLM pretraining optimizers.

The batch-size-one analysis (Section 4.4), which is advertised as revealing a 'fundamentally different implicit bias,' is proven only for a specially constructed 'orthogonal scale-skewed' dataset rather than for general separable data; the generality of this qualitative finding to realistic data is unclear, and the paper itself acknowledges this as a limitation without offering a path to close the gap.

The convergence-rate bounds are extremely complicated, with many case splits (a<1/2, a=1/2, 1/2<a<1, a=1) and constants that scale badly with batch/momentum parameters (e.g., m^{2+a}/(1-β1), (1-β1)^{-2}), and the derivations of these constants rely on further nested lemmas (e.g., Lemma C.15) with their own implicit constants; this makes it hard to assess how tight or practically meaningful these bounds actually are, and raises doubts about whether the qualitative claims (e.g., 'batch-momentum trade-off') would hold non-vacuously in realistic parameter regimes.

The real-data validation is limited to a small two-layer network on a 1000-sample, 10-class MNIST subset, which is far from the large-scale pretraining setting that motivates the paper in the introduction (Adam, Muon for LLMs); the qualitative match to theory is only loosely discussed ('qualitatively consistent') without quantitative comparison to predicted rates.

The overall contribution reads largely as an incremental, if technically thorough, extension of Fan et al. (2025) from full-batch to stochastic steepest descent, and several core messages (stochasticity without stabilization is problematic; momentum/variance-reduction help) are intuitively expected outcomes, so the novelty of the qualitative narrative is more modest than the volume of technical machinery might suggest.

strengths: The paper provides a unified theoretical framework for the implicit bias of mini-batch stochastic steepest descent under general entry-wise and Schatten-p norms, covering SignSGD, Normalized-SGD, Muon, and their momentum/variance-reduced variants as special cases.

The main results are conceptually clean and interesting: it establishes that without momentum, worst-case convergence and successful classification can only be guaranteed in the full-batch regime, backed by a concrete counterexample (Proposition 4.2) showing failure already at m=2 mini-batches, which strengthens the claim beyond a loose sufficient condition.

The momentum analysis (Theorem 4.4) is a genuine technical advance: it removes the dimension dependence present in prior work (Fan et al. 2025), giving dimension-free rates, and explicitly characterizes the batch-size/momentum trade-off governing convergence to an approximate max-margin solution.

The variance-reduction analysis (Theorem 4.7) is a novel contribution showing that SVRG-style correction recovers the exact full-batch max-margin solution regardless of batch size or momentum, at the cost of a slower rate; this is a natural and previously unexplored question that adds insight to the broader picture.

The batch-size-one analysis with an explicitly constructed orthogonal scale-skewed dataset (Theorem 4.10) offers a concrete demonstration that per-sample steepest descent can converge to a fundamentally different implicit bias (governed by class frequency/averaging) than the max-margin solution, illustrating a genuine limitation of the theory.

The paper is thorough in its technical treatment: extensive appendix with detailed proofs, explicit non-asymptotic constants (e.g., closed-form t0 and c2 in Lemma C.15), and extension to exponential loss, indicating strong reproducibility of the theoretical claims.

Experiments on synthetic data and MNIST (two-layer network) are consistent with and support the theoretical predictions across l2, l-infinity, and spectral norms, batch sizes, and momentum settings, lending empirical credibility to the theory.

Related work is well situated relative to recent literature on implicit bias of Adam, Muon, and per-sample optimizers (e.g., Baek et al. 2025), with clear articulation of how this paper's contribution differs (general norm framework, explicit rates, standard random-reshuffling protocol rather than fixed cyclic batches).
weaknesses: The theoretical setting is restricted to linear classifiers on linearly separable data; while this is standard in the implicit bias literature and acknowledged as a limitation, it does somewhat limit the direct applicability of the sharp rates to deep networks (though MNIST experiments provide partial empirical extension).

The batch-size-one implicit bias result (Theorem 4.10) relies on a specially constructed orthogonal dataset, which, while illustrative, does not fully characterize the general implicit bias landscape for arbitrary datasets in the small-batch, no-stabilization regime; the authors acknowledge this but a broader characterization would strengthen the contribution.

The convergence rate bounds, while dimension-free, carry fairly complex dependence on batch-related factors (m^{2+a}, m/(1-beta1), etc.) that could obscure practical interpretability; more discussion or simulation illustrating how tight these rates are in practice would help.

The real-data (MNIST) experiments are relatively limited in scope (single two-layer network, specific class/sample subset) and mostly presented in the appendix; a slightly more extensive empirical evaluation in the main text could better connect the theory to practical training regimes.

Some notational density (e.g., many constants alpha1, alpha2, c1, c2, D) makes the main theorems somewhat hard to parse without cross-referencing the appendix, which could be streamlined for readability.
